property_summary: For any depositor and deposit amount, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract always reduces the contract balance by the withdrawn amount (i.e. address(c).balance decreases by the depositor's credited amount) even if the callee's receive/fallback reverts or runs out of gas; replacing .call with .send can cause the external send to fail and make withdrawAll revert, leaving the contract balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any depositor and any (payable) adversarial recipient contract, the correct C using low-level .call will always forward the owed Ether such that after a successful withdrawAll the contract balance decreases by the withdrawn credit (i.e., withdrawAll returns successfully and address(c).balance == previousBalance - amount); replacing .call with .send can cause the external send to fail for some recipient contracts (which return false) and thus make withdrawAll revert or not transfer funds, violating this property.

For any depositor and any adversarial recipient contract that may revert in its fallback/receive, the reference C always succeeds in withdrawAll (does not revert) because .call forwards enough gas and propagates the callee's behavior as a revert that is bubbled via require(callResult) only if call returned false — but the mutant using .send can return false when the callee runs out of gas or reverts, causing withdrawAll to revert for some inputs; therefore: for all fuzzed depositor and deposit amount and for a deployed reverter helper, calling withdrawAll on the reference never reverts, while the .send-mutant can cause a revert for some inputs.

For any depositor address and deposit amount > 0, calling deposit then withdrawAll on the correct contract (which uses .call) always succeeds (withdrawAll does not revert) even if the recipient's fallback consumes lots of gas or reverts; replacing .call with .send can cause the external send to return false and make withdrawAll revert for some adversarial recipient contracts.

For any depositor address and positive deposit amount, when the depositor calls deposit and then withdrawAll, the reference C (which uses low-level .call and requires the call returned true) will not revert when the recipient's fallback deliberately consumes gas or reenters (because .call forwards gas and preserves behavior), whereas the mutant using .send can cause the external send to fail (return false) for some adversarial recipient behaviors and thus make withdrawAll revert; therefore assert that after a deposit by an EOA and a subsequent withdrawAll invoked via an adversarial contract (which forwards the call to c to trigger the external send), the correct contract's withdrawAll call succeeds (does not revert) for all fuzzed deposit amounts > 0, while the mutant will fail for some such inputs.

For any caller and any deposited amount, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract (which uses low-level call and checks its boolean) always returns (completes) and leaves contract balance decreased by the withdrawn amount when the callee's receive/fallback reverts vs when it accepts — replacing the low-level call with transfer will revert for callees that revert or require more gas, so the mutant can fail to complete while the reference handles the boolean and therefore the reference always completes successfully for the adversarial reverter helper while the mutant does not.

For any caller and any deposited amount, calling withdrawAll always returns (does not revert) on the reference implementation (because it uses a low-level call and checks the boolean) but the mutant that uses transfer will revert when the recipient reverts; the property: withdrawAll call always succeeds on the reference for all inputs while the mutant fails for some adversarial recipient.

For any depositor and deposit amount, calling withdrawAll always returns (does not revert) on the reference C (which uses a low-level call and handles a failing external send by require(callResult) only after resetting state), but replacing the low-level call with transfer() can cause withdrawAll to revert when the recipient reverts — so the property: withdrawAll call always completes (does not revert) for the reference; the transfer-mutant can revert for some adversarial recipient.

For any depositor and any recipient address, calling withdrawAll on the reference C (which uses low-level call and checks its boolean) always completes (does not revert) even if the recipient reverts; the mutant that uses transfer() can revert for some adversarial recipient, breaking this rule.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, calling withdrawAll on the reference C always returns (does not revert) even if the recipient intentionally reverts; replacing the low-level call with transfer can cause withdrawAll to revert when the recipient reverts, so the mutant fails for some recipient that reverts in its fallback/receive.

Invariant: After any withdrawAll() call by any user, the contract's recorded credit for that caller is always 0 (reference zeroes before external call); the mutant that zeroes after the external call can be re-entered to withdraw twice so the credit may remain nonzero or allow double withdrawal, violating the invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and any deposited amount, after they call withdrawAll() the contract's recorded credit for that caller is always zero (reference zeroes before the external call); the mutant that zeroes after the external call can be re-entered and thus can leave credit nonzero or allow double-withdrawal, violating this rule for some inputs.

If a caller deposits >0 and then calls withdrawAll once (even if the callee re-enters), the correct contract will always have its recorded credit for that caller equal to 0 after withdrawAll returns; the mutant that zeroes credit after the external call can be re-entered by a malicious receiver to drain funds and leave inconsistent balance/allow double-withdrawal, violating this property for some adversarial caller and deposit amount.

For any depositor and any positive deposit amount, after they call withdrawAll() the contract's recorded credit for that caller is always zero (the reference zeroes credit before the external call); the mutant that zeroes credit after the external call can be re-entered by a malicious receiver to withdraw twice and thereby violate that the credit is zero after withdrawAll returns for some adversarial caller and amount.

For any depositor and deposit amount > 0, after withdrawAll completes the contract's recorded total balance (address(c).balance) equals the stored internal balance variable; the mutant that omits decrementing internal balance can leave address(c).balance != c.balance() allowing a mismatch.

For any depositor and any positive deposit amount, after the depositor calls withdrawAll the contract's on-chain ether balance (address(c).balance) must equal the contract's reported internal balance getter (c.balance()), but the mutant that omits decrementing the internal balance can make address(c).balance > c.balance() for some inputs (a depositor with positive balance).

For any depositor and deposit amount, after the depositor successfully withdraws all funds the contract's internal recorded balance equals the on-chain ether balance (address(c).balance == c.balance()); the mutant that omits decrementing the internal balance breaks this: for some deposit amounts the balances will differ.

After a depositor with positive credited funds calls withdrawAll, the contract's internal recorded balance (exposed via a public getter) decreases by the withdrawn amount so that address(c).balance == address(c).balance_before - withdrawn AND equals c.balance(); the mutant that omits decrementing the internal balance can leave the internal getter larger than the on-chain balance for some inputs.

For any depositor and deposit amount > 0, after the depositor successfully withdraws all funds, the contract's public getter for the internal accounting variable `balance()` reports the same value as the contract's on-chain Ether balance (address(c).balance) decreased by the withdrawn amount; the mutant that fails to decrement the internal balance can make address(c).balance and c.balance() diverge for some inputs.

For any caller and deposited amount, calling withdrawAll always sets the caller's recorded credit to zero (reference preserves this), but the mutant that zeroes credit at the wrong time can leave credit non-zero when an external call reverts — the reference always ends with credit == 0 while the mutant can end with credit != 0 for some inputs (a callee that reverts).

For any caller and any deposit amount, after withdrawAll returns the contract's stored credit for that caller is always zero (the reference always clears credit even if the external call reverts), whereas the mutant that zeroes credit at the wrong time can leave the caller's credit non-zero when the external call reverts.

For any caller and deposit amount, a successful withdrawAll call on the correct contract always results in the caller's recorded credit being zero afterwards; the mutant that sets credit to zero at the wrong time can leave credit non-zero when the external call reverts, so there exist inputs (a failing/ reverting callee) that make the mutant violate this rule.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, if the external low-level call during withdrawAll fails (reverts), the reference contract P always preserves the contract balance consistent with recorded credits (i.e., address(c).balance == balance field implied by credits) while the mutant M can end up with address(c).balance not matching the stored credit mapping for that caller after a failed external call (because it zeroes credit too early).

For any depositor address and deposit amount, if the depositor calls deposit then withdrawAll and the low-level external call made during withdrawAll REVERTS, the reference C always preserves the depositor's recorded credit (credit remains unchanged) whereas the mutant that zeroes credit at the wrong time can lose/zero the recorded credit despite the external call reverting.
